{ "item": { "id": "6426c6c2-eb67-4e36-acee-0cb4222c0111", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Building your first pipeline", "short_description": "Create a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that connects them, end to end.", "body": "

Building your first pipeline

This guide walks through creating a pipeline end to end: a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that ties them together.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you start|body_html=

You'll need an API key. See Authentication in Getting Started if you don't have one yet.

}}

1. Create a source connector

We'll pull orders from Postgres. See Connectors for the full catalog of types.

Bash / curl

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-source.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \\\n -d '{"type":"postgres","direction":"source","config":{"connection_string":"postgres://..."}}'}}

Go

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=main.go|language=go|code=package main\n\nimport (\n\t"context"\n\t"log"\n\t"os"\n\n\t"github.com/godzilla-io/godzilla-go"\n)\n\nfunc main() {\n\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(os.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY"))\n\n\tsourceConnector, err := client.Connectors.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreateConnectorRequest{\n\t\tType: "postgres",\n\t\tDirection: "source",\n\t\tConfig: map[string]interface{}{\n\t\t\t"connection_string": "postgres://...",\n\t\t},\n\t})\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\tlog.Fatalf("Failed to create source connector: %v", err)\n\t}\n\n\tlog.Printf("Created source connector: %s\\n", sourceConnector.ID)\n}}}

2. Create a destination connector

We'll write to Snowflake.

Bash / curl

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-destination.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \\\n -d '{"type":"snowflake","direction":"destination","config":{"account":"..."}}'}}

Go

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=main.go|language=go|code=package main\n\nimport (\n\t"context"\n\t"log"\n\t"os"\n\n\t"github.com/godzilla-io/godzilla-go"\n)\n\nfunc main() {\n\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(os.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY"))\n\n\tdestinationConnector, err := client.Connectors.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreateConnectorRequest{\n\t\tType: "snowflake",\n\t\tDirection: "destination",\n\t\tConfig: map[string]interface{}{\n\t\t\t"account": "...",\n\t\t},\n\t})\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\tlog.Fatalf("Failed to create destination connector: %v", err)\n\t}\n\n\tlog.Printf("Created destination connector: %s\\n", destinationConnector.ID)\n}}}

3. Create the pipeline

Full request/response details are in the Pipelines endpoint reference.

Bash / curl

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-pipeline.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \\\n -d '{"name":"ingest-orders","source_connector_id":"conn_pg_orders","destination_connector_id":"conn_snowflake_dw"}'}}

Connecting a data source

This guide covers choosing and configuring a source connector — the first step of any new pipeline.

Choosing a connector type

You haveUse
A relational database you can grant replication access toPostgres
Files landing in object storageAmazon S3
An existing event streamKafka
A third party that can push to a URL you controlWebhook

Authenticating

Each connector type has its own credential shape — see the Connectors endpoint for the full parameter list per type.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Least-privilege credentials|body_html=

Grant the connector only the access it needs — read-only replication for Postgres sources, a scoped IAM role for S3, never a superuser or admin credential.

}}

Verifying the connection

A newly created connector reports health: degraded until its first successful read or write, then flips to healthy. If it goes straight to down, double check credentials before opening a support ticket.

Next steps

With a source connected, follow Building your first pipeline to wire it into a full pipeline.

{ "item": { "id": "c98656cb-6460-4f8b-ba79-49ebe476fe49", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Error handling & recovery", "short_description": "How Godzilla retries failed events, when they're dead-lettered, and how to replay them.", "body": "

Handling errors & retries

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={\n "retry_policy": {\n "max_attempts": 5,\n "backoff": "exponential",\n "initial_delay_ms": 1000\n }\n}}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/c40d6d7b-d16a-47f0-979b-086c7f59f113}}|prev_label=Transforming events in flight|next_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|next_label=Scheduling & triggers}}", "version_token": "20bc087d-af58-42fc-b807-e382042a76e4", "created_at": "2026-08-21T15:36:05.867Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-21T15:36:22.705Z", "placement_id": "0b6c15be-6394-4b2e-80ca-660125cbee7b", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "handling-errors-and-retries" } }

{ "item": { "id": "522ba05b-8a21-43dd-82ac-ece908ce14b4", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Monitoring & alerts", "short_description": "Watch pipeline health and get notified of failures via webhooks before they become incidents.", "body": "

Monitoring & alerts

Keep an eye on a running pipeline without babysitting it manually.

Connector health

Poll a connector's health field via the Connectors endpoint, or better, subscribe to connector.error so you're notified the moment it degrades.

Subscribing to pipeline lifecycle events

The most reliable way to monitor a pipeline is a webhook subscription on pipeline.failed and connector.error.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=subscribe.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/webhooks \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"url":"https://you.example.com/hooks/godzilla","events":["pipeline.failed","connector.error"]}'}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=success|title=Recommended baseline|body_html=

At minimum, subscribe to pipeline.failed for every production pipeline. It's the single highest-signal event for catching problems before customers do.

}}

Dead-letter queue depth

A growing dead-letter queue is an early warning sign, not just a symptom — see Handling errors & retries for how events end up there and how to drain them.

{ "item": { "id": "dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Scheduling & triggers", "short_description": "Run a pipeline on a cron schedule or trigger it directly from incoming events.", "body": "

Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=schedule.json|language=json|code={ "schedule": "0 */4 * * *" }}}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

Transforming events in flight

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • Reshaping events
  • Filtering events
  • Enriching events
  • Chaining transforms
  • Monitoring transformations
    • }}

    Once events enter a pipeline, you can reshape their structure, filter out unwanted records, and enrich them with data from external sources — all before they reach the destination. This guide covers the three main transformation patterns.

    Reshaping events

    A reshape transformation maps fields from the source schema into a new output schema. This is useful when your destination expects a different structure than your source provides, or when you want to rename or reorganize fields.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=reshape-transform.json|language=json|code={\\n \"type\": \"reshape\",\\n \"input_schema\": {\\n \"customer_id\": \"string\",\\n \"order_amount\": \"number\",\\n \"timestamp\": \"string\"\\n },\\n \"mappings\": {\\n \"customer_id\": \"customerId\",\\n \"order_amount\": \"totalPrice\",\\n \"timestamp\": \"createdAt\"\\n }\\n}}}

    You can also project only a subset of fields, drop sensitive data before it reaches the destination, or flatten nested structures.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Type coercion|body_html=Reshape transformations can perform basic type conversion: string to number, epoch milliseconds to ISO timestamp, and boolean from string "true"/"false".}}

    Filtering events

    A filter transformation passes events through a condition and drops any that don't match. This prevents your destination from filling up with irrelevant records.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=filter-transform.json|language=json|code={\\n \"type\": \"filter\",\\n \"condition\": {\\n \"field\": \"order_amount\",\\n \"operator\": \"gte\",\\n \"value\": 100\\n }\\n}}}

    Filters support comparison operators (eq, neq, gt, gte, lt, lte), string operations (contains, starts_with, ends_with), and logical combinations using and, or, and not.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Filtered events are dropped|body_html=An event that fails a filter is silently discarded — it doesn't retry, doesn't go to the dead-letter queue, and is not sent to the destination. Use filters when you're confident you want to discard non-matching records.}}

    Enriching events

    An enrichment transformation fetches additional data from an external source (a database, API, or reference table) and adds it to the event payload. This is useful for adding context that the source system doesn't provide.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=enrich-transform.json|language=json|code={\\n \"type\": \"enrich\",\\n \"source\": {\\n \"type\": \"http\",\\n \"url\": \"https://api.example.com/customers/{customer_id}\",\\n \"auth\": \"bearer\"\\n },\\n \"output_field\": \"customer_details\"\\n}}}

    Enrichments extract fields from the event (like a customer ID) to look up external data, then add the response to the event before sending it downstream. If an enrichment request fails or times out, the event retries with the standard backoff policy — see Handling errors & retries for details.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Enrichment adds latency|body_html=Every enrichment HTTP call adds network round-trip time to event processing. For high-volume pipelines, keep enrichment APIs fast or batch-request multiple records at once.}}

    Chaining transforms

    You can apply multiple transforms to a single pipeline in sequence: reshape first to normalize fields, then enrich to add context, then filter to drop unwanted records before they reach the destination.

    Transforms execute in the order you define them, and any error in a transform (including enrichment failures) triggers the standard retry logic. A successful transform passes its output to the next transform in the chain.

    Monitoring transformations

    Track the success rate and latency of each transform in your pipeline's monitoring dashboard. Filter drops are counted separately from errors so you can distinguish between discarded events (which are intentional) and actual failures (which may need attention).

    {{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/3448ffab-598c-46e7-bda6-e7cdc4a1e7c6}}|prev_label=Connecting a data source|next_href={{cms:item/062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c}}|next_label=Handling errors & retries}}

Building your first pipeline

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • Create a source connector
  • Create a destination connector
  • Create the pipeline
  • Next steps
    • }}

    This guide walks through creating a pipeline end to end: a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that ties them together.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you start|body_html=

    You'll need an API key. See Authentication in Getting Started if you don't have one yet.

    }}

    1. Create a source connector

    We'll pull orders from Postgres. See Connectors for the full catalog of types.

    Bash / curl

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-source.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\\\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \\\\\\n -d '{"type":"postgres","direction":"source","config":{"connection_string":"postgres://..."}}'}}

    Go

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=main.go|language=go|code=package main\\n\\nimport (\\n\\t"context"\\n\\t"log"\\n\\t"os"\\n\\n\\t"github.com/godzilla-io/godzilla-go"\\n)\\n\\nfunc main() {\\n\\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(os.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY"))\\n\\n\\tsourceConnector, err := client.Connectors.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreateConnectorRequest{\\n\\t\\tType: "postgres",\\n\\t\\tDirection: "source",\\n\\t\\tConfig: map[string]interface{}{\\n\\t\\t\\t"connection_string": "postgres://...",\\n\\t\\t},\\n\\t})\\n\\tif err != nil {\\n\\t\\tlog.Fatalf("Failed to create source connector: %v", err)\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\tlog.Printf("Created source connector: %s\\\\n", sourceConnector.ID)\\n}}}

    2. Create a destination connector

    We'll write to Snowflake.

    Bash / curl

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-destination.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\\\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \\\\\\n -d '{"type":"snowflake","direction":"destination","config":{"account":"..."}}'}}

    Go

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=main.go|language=go|code=package main\\n\\nimport (\\n\\t"context"\\n\\t"log"\\n\\t"os"\\n\\n\\t"github.com/godzilla-io/godzilla-go"\\n)\\n\\nfunc main() {\\n\\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(os.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY"))\\n\\n\\tdestinationConnector, err := client.Connectors.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreateConnectorRequest{\\n\\t\\tType: "snowflake",\\n\\t\\tDirection: "destination",\\n\\t\\tConfig: map[string]interface{}{\\n\\t\\t\\t"account": "...",\\n\\t\\t},\\n\\t})\\n\\tif err != nil {\\n\\t\\tlog.Fatalf("Failed to create destination connector: %v", err)\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\tlog.Printf("Created destination connector: %s\\\\n", destinationConnector.ID)\\n}}}

    3. Create the pipeline

    Full request/response details are in the Pipelines endpoint reference.

    Bash / curl

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-pipeline.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \\\\\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \\\\\\n -d '{"name":"ingest-orders","source_connector_id":"conn_pg_orders","destination_connector_id":"conn_snowflake_dw"}'}}

    Go

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=main.go|language=go|code=package main\\n\\nimport (\\n\\t"context"\\n\\t"log"\\n\\t"os"\\n\\n\\t"github.com/godzilla-io/godzilla-go"\\n)\\n\\nfunc main() {\\n\\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(os.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY"))\\n\\n\\tpipeline, err := client.Pipelines.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreatePipelineRequest{\\n\\t\\tName: "ingest-orders",\\n\\t\\tSourceConnectorID: "conn_pg_orders",\\n\\t\\tDestinationConnectorID: "conn_snowflake_dw",\\n\\t})\\n\\tif err != nil {\\n\\t\\tlog.Fatalf("Failed to create pipeline: %v", err)\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\tlog.Printf("Created pipeline: %s (state: %s)\\\\n", pipeline.ID, pipeline.State)\\n}}}

    The pipeline starts in draft state. Activate it once you're ready to start processing events.

    Next steps

    Now that events are flowing, read Handling errors & retries to see what happens when a write fails, or Monitoring & alerts to watch it run.

Handling errors & retries

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • Automatic retries
  • Dead-lettering
  • Replaying events
  • Watching for failures
    • }}

    Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

    Automatic retries

    Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={\\n \"retry_policy\": {\\n \"max_attempts\": 5,\\n \"backoff\": \"exponential\",\\n \"initial_delay_ms\": 1000\\n }\\n}}}

    Dead-lettering

    An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

    Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

    }}

    Replaying events

    Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \\\\\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

    Watching for failures

    Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

    {{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/c40d6d7b-d16a-47f0-979b-086c7f59f113}}|prev_label=Transforming events in flight|next_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|next_label=Scheduling & triggers}}
